almanac/calendar.english:
# The calendar: leap years, the lengths of months, and the day of the week.
#
# This is a chapter of the almanac book. The first sentence says which of its
# words other files may use. Everything else here is its own business.

This chapter shares only leapness, month length, month title and weekday.

Let the month row always be "January February March April May June July August September October November December".
Let the day row always be "Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday".

# One word of a row of words, counting from 1.
To work out the pick (text) at a spot (number) of a row (text):
  Let the place be 0.
  For each word in the words of the row:
    Add 1 to the place.
    If the place is the spot:
      The answer is the word.
  Fail because "there is no word {the spot} in ""{the row}""".

# What is left of a count of days when the whole weeks are taken out.
To work out the leftover (number) of a count (number):
  Let the rest be the count.
  While the rest is at least 7:
    Subtract 7 from the rest.
  The answer is the rest.

# A year is a leap year if four divides it, except that a year a hundred
# divides is not, unless four hundred does.
To work out the leapness (yes or no) of a year (number):
  If the year is divisible by 400:
    The answer is yes.
  If the year is divisible by 100:
    The answer is no.
  The answer is whether the year is divisible by 4.

To work out the month length (number) of a month (number) for a year (number):
  If the month is 2:
    If the leapness of the year is yes:
      The answer is 29.
    The answer is 28.
  If the month is 4 or the month is 6 or the month is 9 or the month is 11:
    The answer is 30.
  The answer is 31.

To work out the month title (text) of a month (number):
  The answer is the pick at the month of the month row.

# The day of the week, counted forward from Monday, the first of January 1900.
To work out the weekday (text) of a day (number) at a month (number) for a year (number):
  If the year is less than 1900:
    Fail because "this calendar starts in 1900".
  Let the count be the day - 1.
  Let the passing be 1.
  While the passing is less than the month:
    Add the month length of the passing for the year to the count.
    Add 1 to the passing.
  Let the turning be 1900.
  While the turning is less than the year:
    If the leapness of the turning is yes:
      Add 366 to the count.
    Otherwise:
      Add 365 to the count.
    Set the count to the leftover of the count.
    Add 1 to the turning.
  The answer is the pick at (the leftover of the count + 1) of the day row.

For example, the leapness of 1900 is no and the leapness of 2000 is yes.
For example, the month length of 2 for 2024 is 29.
For example, the weekday of 1 at 1 for 1900 is "Monday".
For example, the weekday of 1 at 1 for 2000 is "Saturday".
almanac/feasts.english:
# The quarter days and some other feasts of the old English year.
#
# A chapter of the almanac book. It uses another chapter of the same book, so
# it names it without saying which book.

This chapter shares only feast, wintry, falling and Michaelmas.

Use the calendar chapter.

A feast has a month (number) and a day (number).

There is a feast called Candlemas whose month is 2 and whose day is 2.
There is a feast called Lady Day whose month is 3 and whose day is 25.
There is a feast called Midsummer whose month is 6 and whose day is 24.
There is a feast called Lammas whose month is 8 and whose day is 1.
There is a feast called Michaelmas whose month is 9 and whose day is 29.
There is a feast called Martinmas whose month is 11 and whose day is 11.
There is a feast called Christmas whose month is 12 and whose day is 25.

A feast is wintry when its month is at most 2 or its month is at least 11.

# The day of the week a feast falls on in a given year.
To work out the falling (text) of a feast for a year (number):
  The answer is the weekday of the feast's day at the feast's month for the year.

For example, the falling of Christmas for 2000 is "Monday".
almanac/numerals.english:
# Roman numerals, into them and out of them.
#
# A chapter of the almanac book. It shares two words. The table of numerals it
# works from is a kind of thing, and that kind is not shared: no other file can
# count the numerals, change one or make another.

This chapter shares only roman and reading.

A numeral has a worth (number) and a sign (text).

There is a numeral called Thousand whose worth is 1,000 and whose sign is "M".
There is a numeral called Ninehundred whose worth is 900 and whose sign is "CM".
There is a numeral called Fivehundred whose worth is 500 and whose sign is "D".
There is a numeral called Fourhundred whose worth is 400 and whose sign is "CD".
There is a numeral called Hundred whose worth is 100 and whose sign is "C".
There is a numeral called Ninety whose worth is 90 and whose sign is "XC".
There is a numeral called Fifty whose worth is 50 and whose sign is "L".
There is a numeral called Forty whose worth is 40 and whose sign is "XL".
There is a numeral called Ten whose worth is 10 and whose sign is "X".
There is a numeral called Nine whose worth is 9 and whose sign is "IX".
There is a numeral called Five whose worth is 5 and whose sign is "V".
There is a numeral called Four whose worth is 4 and whose sign is "IV".
There is a numeral called Unit whose worth is 1 and whose sign is "I".

# Into Roman: take the largest numeral that still fits, as often as it fits.
To work out the roman (text) of a sum (number):
  Let the rest be the sum.
  Let the line be "".
  For each numeral:
    While the rest is at least the numeral's worth:
      Set the line to "{the line}{the numeral's sign}".
      Subtract the numeral's worth from the rest.
  The answer is the line.

# What one Roman letter is worth, or nothing if it is not one.
To work out the weight (number, if any) of a mark (text):
  For each numeral whose sign is the mark:
    The answer is the numeral's worth.
  The answer is nothing.

# Out of Roman: add up the letters, but a letter that stands before a bigger
# one is taken away instead, as the I in IV is.
To work out the reading (number) of a line (text):
  Let the total be 0.
  Let the spot be 0.
  Let the size be the length of the line.
  Repeat the size times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Let the mark be the first 1 letters of the last (the size - the spot + 1) letters of the line.
    Let the here be the weight of the mark.
    If the here is nothing:
      Fail because "{the mark} is not a Roman numeral".
    Let the after be 0.
    If the spot is less than the size:
      Let the following be the first 1 letters of the last (the size - the spot) letters of the line.
      Set the after to the weight of the following or else 0.
    If the here is less than the after:
      Subtract the here from the total.
    Otherwise:
      Add the here to the total.
  The answer is the total.

For example, the roman of 1994 is "MCMXCIV".
For example, the reading of "MCMXCIV" is 1994.
tasks/cards.english:
# What a task is, and how one is written down.
#
# A chapter of the tasks book. A task is a card of the page library. This
# chapter adds what the library does not know: when a card counts as open, how
# the words that were typed become a card, and what order cards stand in.

This chapter shares only open, twin and jot.

Use the page library.
Use the layout chapter.

A card is open when it is not ticked.

# The card that already says this, if there is one.
To work out the twin (card, if any) of a phrase (text):
  For each card whose wording is the phrase:
    The answer is the card.
  The answer is nothing.

# Write a new card from what was typed. A word that begins with # is the
# card's tag and is left out of its wording, so "Buy milk #home" becomes the
# card "Buy milk", tagged "home". Nothing is written twice, and nothing blank.
To jot a line (text):
  Let the phrase be "".
  Let the mark (text, if any) be nothing.
  For each word in the words of the line:
    If the word starts with "#":
      If the length of the word is more than 1:
        Set the mark to the last (the length of the word - 1) letters of the word.
    Otherwise if the phrase is "":
      Set the phrase to the word.
    Otherwise:
      Set the phrase to "{the phrase} {the word}".
  If the phrase is "":
    Fail because "there is nothing to write down".
  If the twin of the phrase is not nothing:
    Fail because """{the phrase}"" is on the list already".
  Let the card be a new card whose wording is the phrase and whose panel is Roll.
  If the mark is not nothing:
    Set the card's tag to the mark.

# Starred cards stand first and finished ones last. Among cards of the same
# sort, the one written first stands first: the page keeps that order itself.
To work out the standing (number) of a card:
  If the card is ticked:
    The answer is 2.
  If the card is starred:
    The answer is 0.
  The answer is 1.

Keep each card's order as the standing of the card.
tasks/keeping.english:
# What is remembered: the whole list between visits, and the last card removed.
#
# A chapter of the tasks book. A card is kept as one line of text:
#
#     x * home Buy milk
#
# The first word is x if it is done, the second is * if it is starred, the
# third is its tag, and the rest is its wording. A dash stands for "no". How a
# card is kept is this chapter's own business: the other files only ask it to
# save the list, fetch it, shelve a card or restore one, and whether one is spare.

This chapter shares only save, fetch, shelve, restore and sparing.

Use the page library.
Use the layout chapter.

# The last card removed, as a line, until it is put back.
Let the spare (text, if any) be nothing.

# The list as it was last written. No list is ever these two words.
Let the written be "nothing yet".

# A card as a line of text.
To work out the listing (text) of a card:
  Let the tick be "-".
  If the card is ticked:
    Set the tick to "x".
  Let the star be "-".
  If the card is starred:
    Set the star to "*".
  Let the mark be the card's tag or else "-".
  The answer is "{the tick} {the star} {the mark} {the card's wording}".

# A line of text as a card again.
To revive a line (text):
  Let the place be 0.
  Let the tick be "-".
  Let the star be "-".
  Let the mark be "-".
  Let the phrase be "".
  For each word in the words of the line:
    Add 1 to the place.
    If the place is 1:
      Set the tick to the word.
    Otherwise if the place is 2:
      Set the star to the word.
    Otherwise if the place is 3:
      Set the mark to the word.
    Otherwise if the phrase is "":
      Set the phrase to the word.
    Otherwise:
      Set the phrase to "{the phrase} {the word}".
  If the phrase is "":
    Stop.
  Let the card be a new card whose wording is the phrase and whose panel is Roll.
  If the mark is not "-":
    Set the card's tag to the mark.
  If the star is "*":
    Now the card is starred.
  If the tick is "x":
    Now the card is ticked.

# Save the whole list in the browser, for next time. It is written only when
# it differs from what was written last, so a letter typed in a box saves nothing.
To save:
  Let the record be "".
  For each card:
    Set the record to "{the record}{the listing of the card}{new line}".
  If the record is the written:
    Stop.
  Remember the record under "tasks".
  Set the written to the record.

# Bring back the list as it was left. On a first visit there is none, so
# three cards are written to begin with.
To fetch:
  Let the saved be the memory of "tasks".
  If the saved is nothing:
    Revive "- - - Read the treatise".
    Revive "- * - Write a sentence the compiler refuses".
    Revive "- - page Tick this one off".
  Otherwise:
    For each line in the lines of the saved:
      Revive the line.

# Is there a card that can be put back?
To work out the sparing (yes or no):
  The answer is whether the spare is not nothing.

# Remove a card, keeping it as the one that can be put back.
To shelve a card:
  Set the spare to the listing of the card.
  Remove the card.

# Put the last card removed back on the list.
To restore:
  If the spare is nothing:
    Stop.
  Revive the spare.
  Set the spare to nothing.
tasks/layout.english:
# What is on the page, from top to bottom.
#
# A chapter of the tasks book. Each thing made here is an element of the page.
# The other chapters change these things by name, so the names they need are
# shared. The panels that only hold things in place are not.

This chapter shares only Entry, Adder, Notice, Everything, Waiting, Finished, Finder, Roll, Tally, Progress, Finisher, Sweeper and Restorer.

Use the page library.

There is a heading called Banner whose wording is "Things to do".

# Where a new task is written.
There is a panel called Desk.
There is a field called Entry whose wording is "" and whose hint is "What needs doing? Add a #tag if you like." and whose panel is Desk.
There is a button called Adder whose label is "Add" and whose panel is Desk.

# A line for telling the reader something: why a task was not added, or that one can be put back.
There is a note called Notice whose wording is "".

# Which tasks are in sight.
There is a panel called Sieve.
There is a button called Everything whose label is "All" and whose panel is Sieve.
There is a button called Waiting whose label is "Still to do" and whose panel is Sieve.
There is a button called Finished whose label is "Done" and whose panel is Sieve.
There is a field called Finder whose wording is "" and whose hint is "Find" and whose panel is Sieve.

# The cards go here, as they are made.
There is a panel called Roll.

There is a panel called Foot.
There is a note called Tally whose wording is "" and whose panel is Foot.
There is a gauge called Progress whose level is 0 and whose limit is 1 and whose panel is Foot.

# Things to do to the whole list.
There is a panel called Shelf.
There is a button called Finisher whose label is "Tick them all" and whose panel is Shelf.
There is a button called Sweeper whose label is "Clear what is done" and whose panel is Shelf.
There is a button called Restorer whose label is "Put the last one back" and whose panel is Shelf.
tasks/showing.english:
# Which cards are in sight, and what the page says about them.
#
# A chapter of the tasks book. Nothing here is done by hand. Each sentence
# beginning "Keep" says what something on the page is always to be, and the
# language keeps it so after every change, however the change came about.
#
# The chapter keeps one thing to itself: which of the three views is in force.
# No other file can read that or change it, except by asking this chapter to
# "favour" a view.

This chapter shares only favour.

Use the page library.
Use the layout chapter.
Use the cards chapter.
Use the keeping chapter.

# The view in force: "all", "open" or "done".
Let the showing be "all".

To favour a pick (button) for a choice (text):
  For each button:
    Now the button is not chosen.
  Now the pick is chosen.
  Set the showing to the choice.

# What the Find box is matched against: a card's words and its tag, without
# regard to capitals.
To work out the matter (text) of a card:
  If the card has a tag:
    The answer is "{the card's wording in lower case} #{the card's tag in lower case}".
  The answer is the card's wording in lower case.

To work out the sought (text):
  The answer is Finder's wording in lower case.

# A card is out of sight when the view leaves it out, or the Find box does not
# match it.
Keep each card hidden when (the showing is "open" and the card is ticked) or (the showing is "done" and the card is open) or the matter of the card does not contain the sought.

# The counts, wherever the page shows one.
Keep Everything's label as "All ({the number of cards})".
Keep Waiting's label as "Still to do ({the number of open cards})".
Keep Finished's label as "Done ({the number of ticked cards})".
Keep Progress's level as the number of ticked cards.
Keep Progress's limit as the number of cards.

To work out the verdict (text):
  Let the whole be the number of cards.
  Let the remaining be the number of open cards.
  If the whole is 0:
    The answer is "Nothing to do. Write something above."
  If the remaining is 0:
    The answer is "All {the whole} done."
  The answer is "{the remaining} of {the whole} still to do."

Keep Tally's wording as the verdict.

# A button that would do nothing is put out of sight.
Keep each button hidden when (the button is Finisher and the number of open cards is 0) or (the button is Sweeper and the number of ticked cards is 0) or (the button is Restorer and the sparing is no).
